title: GCD and OperationQueue basics (and how they compare to async/await)
summary: GCD runs blocks of work on queues: the main queue for UI, background queues for heavy work. Swift concurrency (async/await) is the modern replacement, but GCD is still asked in every interview.
body: **In simple words:** A thread is a worker. A queue is a to-do list. With GCD you do not manage threads yourself; you put closures on a queue and GCD picks a worker to run them.

**Serial vs concurrent queue:** a serial queue runs one task at a time, in order (like one cashier). A concurrent queue can run many at once (several cashiers). The **main queue** is serial and is the only place to update UI.

**sync vs async:** `async` = "add to the queue and continue, do not wait". `sync` = "add and wait until it finishes". Calling `DispatchQueue.main.sync` from the main thread deadlocks: main waits for itself.
**QoS (priority):** `.userInteractive` (animations), `.userInitiated` (user is waiting), `.utility` (long, with progress), `.background` (user does not notice).

**Other tools:** `DispatchGroup` waits for several tasks to finish, `asyncAfter` delays work, a **barrier** on a concurrent queue gives "many readers, one writer". `OperationQueue` adds dependencies between operations, cancellation and `maxConcurrentOperationCount`.

**Why async/await is better now:** GCD spawns more threads when work blocks, which can cause **thread explosion** (many threads, lots of memory and switching). Swift concurrency uses a small fixed pool (about one thread per CPU core) and suspends instead of blocking. It also checks data races at compile time.
keyPoints: Main queue = serial, UI only. Global queues = concurrent with QoS levels.
`async` does not wait; `sync` waits. `main.sync` from main = deadlock.
Serial queue protects state by running one block at a time; barrier = reader-writer lock.
Swift concurrency avoids thread explosion by suspending instead of blocking.

code.caption: Common GCD patterns

mistakes: Updating UI from a background queue (random crashes and glitches).
Calling `sync` on the queue you are already on (deadlock).
Using `DispatchSemaphore.wait()` inside async code (can deadlock the cooperative pool).
followups: **Is a serial queue the same as the main thread?** No. The main queue is one special serial queue; other serial queues run on any background thread.
**What is thread explosion?** GCD creating too many threads because tasks block; each thread costs memory and context switches.
**When would you still use OperationQueue?** When tasks need dependencies (B after A) and cancellation in legacy code.
**Difference between concurrency and parallelism?** Concurrency = dealing with many tasks at once (can interleave on one core); parallelism = actually running at the same time on multiple cores.
